prompt: Why is a rule written for Snort, most of the time, also a rule for Suricata?
hint: What did Suricata choose to read in 2010?

choices.text: Both engines are built from the same source code
choices.why: They are separate programs; they share the rule language.

choices.text: Suricata was deliberately built to read Snort's rules
choices.why: Right. The shared language is the useful fact.

choices.text: Suricata converts Snort rules to YAML when it loads them
choices.why: YAML is its configuration, not its rule format.

choices.text: Rules describe ports, and ports are the same everywhere
choices.why: The reason is the language; rules describe far more than ports.

prompt: Match each engine to how it is configured.
A defender has to choose one engine and wants to find things no rule was written for. What difference in the table matters most?

choices.text: Suricata is multi-threaded, and Snort 2 runs one thread per process
choices.why: That is speed, not what gets recorded.

choices.text: Suricata's rules are longer
choices.why: The rule language is essentially shared.

choices.text: Suricata records HTTP, DNS and TLS whether or not a rule matched
choices.why: Right. Those records are what anomalies are found in.

choices.text: Snort 3 is configured in Lua
choices.why: The configuration language finds nothing.

prompt: Which of these belong in local rules rather than in a published rule set? Choose all that apply.
hint: What does only this network know?

choices.text: Which paths on the company's site are private
choices.why: Right. Nobody outside knows them.

choices.text: A signature for a malware family seen worldwide
choices.why: Published sets are maintained for that, and updated daily.

choices.text: Which protocols have no business on which segment
choices.why: Right. That is this network's own layout.

choices.text: Which login form is sensitive
choices.why: Right, like the rule in this lesson.

choices.text: An exploit against a widely used web server
choices.why: Known exploits are what published sets carry.

prompt: The rule puts http.uri before content:"/login". A request to /shop sends a cookie containing /login. Does it match?
hint: Where does a content search after a sticky buffer?

choices.text: Yes, because /login appears in the request
choices.why: That is what a content with no buffer would do.

choices.text: Yes, because cookies are part of the URI
choices.why: A cookie is a header, outside the path.

choices.text: No: the content is searched in the path
choices.why: Right. And the path is /shop.

choices.text: No, because the method was not checked first
choices.why: The method check is separate from where /login is searched.

prompt: The team changes the count in rule 1000201 from 10 to 20. What should happen to rev, and why?

choices.text: Nothing: rev counts how often the rule fired
choices.why: rev is written by the author, not counted by the engine.

choices.text: sid is raised instead, since it is a new rule
choices.why: It is the same rule in a new version.

choices.text: rev is set to 20, to match the count
choices.why: rev is a revision number, unrelated to the count.

choices.text: It becomes 2, so an alert names the version that produced it
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Order the steps the lesson took on sensor, from first to last.
hint: A rule file is tested before anything runs.
items: list the file under rule-files in suricata.yaml
start the engine on the DMZ interface
trap: Starting first means a mistake in a rule is found by the engine in production.

prompt: remote posted the login form fifteen times, under detection_filter with count 10. How many alerts did fast.log hold for sid 1000201?
Match each counting keyword to when it fires.

pairs.right: on each match after the count is exceeded
at most N times per period

prompt: A rule is right, but during a scan it fires hundreds of times. The analyst wants to know the scan started and not the rest. Which keyword answers that?

choices.text: threshold: type limit
choices.why: Right. At most N alerts per period.

choices.text: detection_filter
choices.why: It keeps alerting on each match past the count.

choices.text: threshold: type threshold, to see the volume
choices.why: One per N shows the volume, which the analyst said they do not need.

choices.text: Deleting the rule until the scan ends
choices.why: That loses the start as well.

prompt: The first two alerts from remote carry the same second, 18:03:37. What does that suggest?
hint: Could a person type that fast?

choices.text: The sensor's clock is wrong
choices.why: A wrong clock would shift both, not make them equal.

choices.text: The alert was written twice for one request
choices.why: Fifteen requests, five alerts: one each for 11 to 15.

choices.text: A script
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The proxy retried a failed request
choices.why: Every request got 200.

prompt: Rule 2221014 fired on remote's request with no Host header. Who described that request?

choices.text: The lesson's author, in local.rules
choices.why: local.rules holds 1000201 alone.

choices.text: The proxy, which reported it to the sensor with its 400
choices.why: The sensor watches traffic; the proxy tells it nothing.

choices.text: Nobody: the parser knows what a valid request is
choices.why: Right. http-events.rules turns its events into alerts.

choices.text: Emerging Threats Open
choices.why: It ships with Suricata, not with that set.

prompt: How many DNS questions did the sensor record from 203.0.113.50?
Finding what departs from a machine's normal behaviour, rather than what somebody described in a signature, is ___ detection.
Why is malformed HTTP a useful signal even when nothing in it is harmful?

choices.text: It crashes the proxy
choices.why: The proxy answered 400 and carried on.

choices.text: Ordinary clients do not send it; scanners and hand-made tools do
choices.why: Right. Its source is the signal.

choices.text: Malformed requests carry malware
choices.why: This one carried a missing header and no payload.

choices.text: It proves the sender is inside the company
choices.why: It came from 203.0.113.50, outside.

prompt: 203.0.113.50 asked the public name server for www, shop, mail, vpn and six more names. Why would no signature fire on it?
hint: Look at one question on its own.

choices.text: DNS travels over UDP, which rules do not inspect
choices.why: Suricata parsed and recorded every question.

choices.text: The questions were encrypted
choices.why: The sensor read every name in them.

choices.text: Ten questions stay under detection_filter's count
choices.why: That count belongs to the login rule, not to DNS.

choices.text: Each was a legitimate question; the pattern is in the count
choices.why: Right.

prompt: The office resolver sees ten names from one laptop in a minute. The public name server sees ten from a stranger. Why can the same number mean different things?
hint: What says whether ten is a lot?

choices.text: Each has its own baseline
choices.why: Right. An office on a Tuesday against a survey.

choices.text: The laptop is inside, and inside traffic is trusted by the sensor
choices.why: The sensor records both the same way.

choices.text: A resolver ignores repeated names
choices.why: These were ten different names.

choices.text: The public server logs more detail than the resolver does
choices.why: The records are the sensor's, in eve.json.

prompt: After the suppress line was loaded, branch posted the form fifteen times. What did eve.json show for sid 1000201?

choices.text: Five alerts from 203.0.113.70 and five from 203.0.113.50
choices.why: The branch's five were suppressed.

choices.text: remote's five alerts, and none from the branch
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: No alerts, because the rule was reloaded
choices.why: Reloading kept remote's earlier alerts and the rule.

choices.text: One alert from the branch, as a reminder
choices.why: suppress writes none for that source.

prompt: How did the lesson load the new threshold file without stopping Suricata?
hint: What was sent to the process?

choices.text: suricata -T, which loads what it tests
choices.why: -T tests and exits.

choices.text: By restarting the sensor machine
choices.why: That stops the engine.

choices.text: The signal USR2
choices.why: Right. The log says rule reload complete.

choices.text: By editing rule 1000201 and raising rev
choices.why: The rule was left untouched.

prompt: Why does a suppression carry who made it, why, and a review date?
hint: What happens to the address later?

choices.text: Suricata refuses a suppress line with no comment
choices.why: The engine reads the line, not the comment.

choices.text: So the rule's rev can be raised to match
choices.why: The rule is untouched by a suppression.

choices.text: Its reason expires and the address becomes a gap
choices.why: Right. Whoever uses it later is unseen.

choices.text: For an auditor to count the alerts that were silenced
choices.why: The point is knowing when to remove it.

prompt: Order the tuning tools from narrowest to broadest.
items: a threshold in the threshold file
trap: Disabling first silences the signal with the noise.

prompt: A local rule has content:"passwd" with no buffer, and it fires all day on a product page describing a password manager. What is the fix?
hint: Is one source to blame, or the rule?

choices.text: Suppress it for the web server's address
choices.why: That hides a real match on that server as well.

choices.text: A threshold of one alert per hundred
choices.why: The rule is too broad, not too frequent.

choices.text: Edit it to search inside http.uri
choices.why: Right. Editing a rule that is too broad.

choices.text: Disable it and rely on Emerging Threats
choices.why: A published set knows no local paths.

prompt: A workstation that asks the resolver for about forty names a day asks for three thousand different ones one night. Which part of this lesson catches it?
hint: Is there a signature for it?

choices.text: A published rule set, updated daily
choices.why: Each name is an ordinary question; there is no signature.

choices.text: A protocol anomaly from http-events.rules
choices.why: The questions are valid DNS, and that file is about HTTP.

choices.text: detection_filter on rule 1000201
choices.why: That rule counts login posts.

choices.text: Counting DNS records against its baseline
choices.why: Right. Forty a day is the baseline.
